ulnaorfocilemajus.c: ULNA, or Focile Majus, is the greater Bone betwixt the Arm and the Wrist, which is jointed upward with the Shoulder by Gingbymus ( which fee; ) and therefore it has there both Processes and Ca - vities; two Oblong Processes, and as it were train - gular, and rugged,, that the Ligaments may knit it strongly. The foremost and uppermost is less, and goes into the Cavity of the Shoulder: The back - ward Process is thicker and larger, ends in an Ob - use Angle, and enters the hinder Cavity of the Shoulder; the Latines call it Gibberus: In the middle of these there ’ s a great Cavity like a Semi - circle. It has yet another external lateral Cavity for the Head of the Radius, or lesser Bone of the Cu - bit; it is jointed at the lower end with the Wrist, both by a Cartilage in the middle, and by an acute Process, and therefore called Styloides ( being like a sharp - pointed Pen used in Writing - Fables ) whence there arises a Ligament, which fattens the Cubit, and the Joint of the Wrist together.

umbelicus.c: UMBELICUS in an Ellipjis, &c. is that Focus about which the Motion of any Revolving Body is made, and which it rcfpecls as its Centre. So that either Focus may be called by this Name.

umbelliferousplants.c: UMBELLIFEROUS Plants, are by Botanijls accounted, such as have their Tops branched and spread out like a Ladies Vmbrella on each little Sub - division of which, there is a small Flower growing: As Fennel, Dill, Parjley, c c. ' This Flower is always Pentapetalous, and is suc - weeded by z Naked Seeds lying joined together, which are the true Diftindfions of these Plants from ethers The Umbelliferous are a very large Genus of Plants, and by our Accurate Botanist Mr. Ray are thus distinguished. Umbelliferous Plants, are either I. Such as have a Compounded Leaf, of a Tri - angular and Pinnate Form: And the Seeds of these are either, a. Broad, flat, and plain, like Leaves almost; as the Sphondylium, Paftinaca Latifolia, Pa - Max Heracleum Tordylium, Orcofelinum, Says - felinum, Apium Cicutce foliis, Daucus Alfati - cus, Cdrvifolia, Anethum, Pucedanum, Thapfia, Ferula, cc. z, With a Seed more Tumid, and less compress - fed and flat than the former: As the Cachrys, Laferpitium, Cicutaria vulgaris, Scandix, Ce - refolium, Myrrhis Sativa Angelica, Levijlicum, Silver Montanum, Bulbocaflunum, Sifarum, Oe - nanthe, Slum, Pimpinella Apium, Cicuta, Vis - aga, Saxifraga, Crithmum, Fceniculum, Dau - cus Vulgaris, Anifum, Caucalci, Coriandrum Pafiifiaca Marina, See. , jo st -, ' u in j r ' i; u, II. Such as have a Simple, or an Undivided Leaf, or at least one, only. a little jagged: As the Perfoliata; Buplerum, Ajlrantia Nigra, Sanicula, and the Seseli /. Ethiopians,

umbelicalregion.c: UMBELICAL Region, is that part of the Abdo - men lying round about the Navel.

umbelicalvessels.c: UMBELICAL Vessels, are the Veins, Arteries, c c. that belong to the Navel, or rather are en - wrapped in the Navel - String. The Navel - string is Membranous, wreathed, and unequal, arising out of the middle of the Ab - women, ( vi. the Navel ) and reaching to the Pla - cent Uterina ’ Tis usually half an Ell in Length, and as thick as ones Finger. It was convenient to be so long and lax, that when the Foetus in the Womb grows strong, it might not break it by its sprawling and tumbling about; and after it is born, the Secundine, or After - birth, might be drawn out the. better by it. The way that it passes from the Navel, to the Placenta, is very unconstant; for sometimes it goes upon the Right hand to the Neck, which ha - ving encompassed, it descends to the Placenta, and sometimes it goes on the Left hand up to the Neck, &c. Sometimes it comes not to the Neck at all, but goes first a little up towards its Breast, and then turns round its Back, and from thence passes to the Placenta. The Vessels contain ’ d in this String, ( and which are enwrapped to a common Coat, called Funicu - lus, or Intefiinulum ) are four, one Vein, two Ar - teries, and the Urachus. For as for the Nerves which Vcrheyen fufpedts to be contained in it, or the LaEleal Vessels which Bidloo thinks he has observed I shall not reckon them among these Vessels, be - cause these Authors speak but faintly of them. The Vein is larger than the Arteries, and arises from the Liver of the Foetus, ( vi. out of its FifliireJ by the Trunk of the Vena Porta ( of which it seems to be but a Branch ) and from thence palling out of the Navel, it runs along the Funiculus to the Placenta, into which it is implanted by innumera - ble Roots; but in its passage it fends some little Twigs into the Arteries. The Ancients, that thought the Foetus was houri - ’ ftied by the Mothers Blood only, taught the some use of this Vein to be, to carry Blood from the Pla - cent to it: And since it has been found out, and believed that it is nourifhecj, also ( if not only ) by Chyle, or Succus Nutritius j some have continued the fame Office to. this Vein, and think that the Chyle is brought by Ladeal Vessels arising out of the Placenta, as ( they fay ) it was brought thither by the Mothers La & ears. And indeed if any cer - tain Discovery had been made of these fame La - Piece, we fhouldhave embraced this Opinion as the most probable. But we are not to form Hypotheses out of Rational Notions only, but much rather from what appears to the Eyes of the Difledor. We do affirm therefore. That the Umbelical Vein serves for conveying to the Foetus the - Nutriti - tious Juice separated in the Placenta from the Mo - thers Arteries. How this Separation is made, and how it is first of all turned into Blood, we shall confider by and bye. But together with this Juice there returns so much of the Arterial Blood ( that comes from the Foetus ) as is not spent upon the Nourishment of the Placenta, or of the Chorion and Amnios: Which Liquors thus mixed, though by the Umbelical Vein, they are poured into the Sinus of the. Porta, yet are they not distributed through the Liver by the usual Channels thereof only, but by the Venal Dud, is the greatest part thereof conveyed in a i diredi UM U M B direct course and full Stream into the Cava about the Liver. Besides this Vein, which is common to all Area - tures, there hav, e been observ ’ d in Whelps and Co - neys, ( and may perhaps in others; two small Veins more, that arising from the fourth involving, Membrane peculiar to them, pass directly from the Vmbelicus to the Mifentery of the Fwtus, as the other great one does to its Liver; which may strengthen the Opinion, That the Chyle, or Suc - cus Nutritius is brought to the Foetus by the Umbi - lical Vein, ( or Veins. ) These Veins Dr. Needham calls Omphalo - Adefentcricw. In the Funiculus are included also two Arteries, which are not both of them together so big as the Vein: They spring out of the inner Iliacal Bran - ches of the great Artery: ( Dr. Needham judges them to be derived immediately from the Extre - mity of the Aorta, before its Division ) and palling by the Sides of the Bladder, they rife up to the Navel, out of which they are conducted to the Placenta, in the lame common cover with the Vein and Urachus, with which they are twined and wreathed not unlike a Rope. I fay, they are iniertedinto the Placenta, and with the Vein make a most admirable Net - like Texture. But there is one Branch of each of them which is manifestly inferred into the Amnios. Dr. Harvey says, The Vein is conspicuous a pretty while before these ’ Arteries appear. In the Creatures mention ’ d in the foregoing Pa - ragraph, there are besides these Arteries, others an - swerving to, and accompanying the Veins called, Ompha lo - Me f enter i ca, abovementioned. Blood and Vital Spirit are not carried by them from the Mother to the Foetus, as many from Galen have taught but on the contrary, Spirituous Blood is driven from, the Foetus, by the beating of its Heart, to the Placenta and the Membranes for their Refedfion and Nourishment j from which what Blood remains, circulates back again in the Umbilical Vein together with th eSuccus Nutritius afrefti imbibed by its Capillaries dispersed in the Placenta. But besides Arterial Blood, there flows out of the Navel by them, part of the Succus Nu - tritius, that was imported by the Umbilical Vein; namely, That of it which is more crass and ter - rent, which by one Circulation through rhe Heart, ( or it may be many ) could not be changed into Blood: This part, I fay, flows out by these Arte - ries, which by their Branches that are dispersed through the Amnios, disembogue it by their little Mouths into it: Spr what Use, shall be declared presently. But besides these Uses which are commonly ascribed to these Umbilical Veins and Arteries by Anatomists, Verheyen ( with some probability ) al - signs another. Says he, “ It is worth Inquiry, for what pur - pose the Blood of the Foetus is sent in such great quantity out of its Body into the Placenta: See - ing, without doubt, a far less quantity of Blood would suffice for its Nourishment: For no part “ in the whole Body, if you except the Lungs and Liver, has such abundance of Blood - Vessels as “ the Placenta. This must needs be for a certain u common Use, which we judge to be a kin to the tile of the Lungs, in thole who being Born, enjoy a freer Air: Namely, That as these do “ by the help of the Lungs plentifully draw in from the Air a certain Matter highly necessary for the H feeding the Vital Flame, so in, the Foetus, where “ the Lungs lie idle, such like Matter being reel “ ved into the Mothers Blood by her Respiration ' ] is separated therefrom by help of the Placenta ) “ and mixt with the Blood of the Foetus ( in the “ Umbilical Vein ) and as in the Lungs of Breath - “ ing Persons, some Heterogenous Matter is con - ' “ continually Separated from the Blood; so in the “ Placenta certain Recrements of rhe Blood are de - “ polited out of the Umbilical Arteries into rhe “ Veins of the Mother. And here I shall Transcribe a Material Objection, with the Answer to it, out of Dicmerbroech Objection. How can these Vessels, ( Vein and Arteries ) when they have grown from the Belly of the Foetus, to that length as to reach the Membranes, penetrate and pass through them to the Placenta ? Answer. This is done in the fame manner as the Roots of Herbs, Shrubs and Trees penetrate into the hard Ground, yea, often into thick Planks, Walls and Stones, ( which Water cannot enter ) and root themselves firmly in them. For just so the first sharp pointed and most find ends of the Umbilical Vessels, insinuate themselves by little and little into, the Pores of the Membranes ( for the Figuration of thole Pores are fitted for their Entrance; and pass through them, and yet the Liquors contained in these Membranes cannot flow out by them: And when those Vessels inhering in the Pores, grow more out into length, by little and little, the said Pores are more and more widened, ( according to the encrease of the Vessels ) and are inseparably u - nited unto, and grow in them. The fourth Umbilical Veffd, is the Urachus, or Urinary Vessel. This is a small, membranous, round Pipe, endowed with a very streight Cavity, arising from the bottom of the Bladder up to the Navel, out of which it passes along within the common cover, and, opens into the Allantoides. It is more apparently pervious in many of the larger Brutes, than it is in Man - in whom some have denied it any Cavity; but that it is hollow in him, is confirmed by many Hiftories of Persons adult, who having the ordinary Urinary Passage along the Penis stopt, the Passage in this Vessel has been unlocked, and they have made Water by the Navel, which could not have been imagined to have happen ’ d, if it had been originally a Liga - ment without any Meatus. Bartholin, and others have affirmed. That the Urachus in Men reaches no further than the Na - vel: How then comes that Humour into the Al - lantoides, chat has perfectly the fame Taste with the Urine in the Bladder ? But their Error sprung from hence, That they thought a Humane Foetus had no Allantoides, and that Humour that is found in it, they thought had been contained in the Chorion. But this is in short refuted above, but more fully and accurately by Dr. Needham, Lib. de sorbate Foetus, cap.. As to the Perviousness of the Urachus, I shall add this farther. That in Abortions of five or fix Months old, the Bladder of the Embryo is always full of Urine, out of which, if m the following Months it should not be emptied by the Urachus t the Bladder would soon burst, seeing there is daily some U N C U N I feme Serum separated from the Blood in the Kid - neys, and sent to the Bladder; and the more the Foetus encreases, the more mull need be separated. Yea, Dr. Needham affirms,. That one may either prels the Liquor contained in the Allantoides by the ' Urachus into the Bladder, and with a Pipe blow Wind out of the Bladder by the fame way into the Allantoides. Its Use has ' been Efficiently declared ia the pre - ceding Paragraph as alio above, when we deli - vered the Use of the Allantoides, which we hall not repeat. These four Vessels ( as has been said above ) have one common cover, which also keeps each of them from touching other. It is called Intejlinulum and Funiculus, ( by which it with its Vessels is some - times understood. ) It is Membranous, round and hollow, indifferent thick, confiding of a double Coat, ( the inner from the Peritoneum, and the outer from the Panniculus carnosus. ) Sometimes it self only is wreathed about like a Rope, the Vessels included in it running streight along its Cavity; and sometimes they are wreathed toge - ther with it. It hath leveral Kjiots upon it here and there, which Dr. Wharton thinks to be Papilla !, or little Glands through which the Ladleal ( or Nutritious Juice ) distill out of the Capacity of the Funiculus, into the Cavity of the Amnios. I cannot tell whether this be so, or no; but the Use that doting Midwives make of them to guess by their Number how many Children more the Mother shall have, and by their Colour, whe - ther those Children ( hall be Male or Female, is more ridiculous than superstitious.

uncoreprism.c: UNCORE Prism, in Law, is a Plea for the De - & idant, being sued for a Debt due at a Day past, to lave the Forfeiture of his Bond, saying, That he rendred the Debt at the Time and Place, and that there was none to receive, and that he is still ready to pay the fame.

unguisanail.c: UNGUIS, a Nail, is a similar, flexible, white,, and hard part, which defends the Fingers from ex - ternal Injuries, and in some measure adorns them. The Root of it is joined to a certain Ligaments, and by reason of the Neighbouring Tendons it be - comes sensible: They seem to be made of a Coh le & ion of Very little Pipes, which adhere extreme - ly thick to one another, and Ihoot out into lengths Where they begin, there you find certain Nervous Fibres like so many small Nipples lengthen ’ d, the lengthen ’ d Parts whereof, are seen as far as the Nail: If they be forcibly torn off, they leave di - vers Holes, so that the Horney Substance of the Nails looks like a Net. Under the Nails there ’ s a Pappy fort of Body, which has its Vessels of Ex creation. The Apices, or Tops of the Nails, are they which grow beyond the Flesh; the parts which are out, are called the Segmina, the Paring of the Nails; the Parts under the Nails, are the K vvrjd, the hidden Parts; the white Semi - lunar part next the Root, if the Rife of the Nail - the very Begin - nings that grow into the Skin, are call ’ d the Roots of the Nail j the Sides, the Clefts; the white Spots, Nubecula, little Clouds, &c. Blanchard.

UNION, Dr. Grew makes Union in a Physical Sense, to be one of the three ways of Mixture and he defines it to be the Union of Atoms, or Par - titles which touch in a Plain; as in the Chryftalli zation of Salts, and other like Bodies.

UNION of two Churches, is a Consolidating or Combining them into one, which may be done by the Consent of the Bishop, Patron, and In - cumbent. See Linwoods Provincials, and H., c. i. as also Car. c..

unisoninmusick.c: UNISON, in Musick, is one or the fame Sound, whether produced by one single Voice, or divers Voices sounding in the fame Tone; so that an V - unison in this Science, may be considered as an U niterln Arithmetick, or as a Point in Geometry, not divisible into any Parts, in regard that it is the siss Term to any Interval. When the Ancients divided their Monochord, so that the Parts were as to r, they called them Vnifons.

unite.c: UNITE, is the fame with the Figure i, being one single individual part of discreet Quantity. If a Number consist of or Places, that which is outermost towards the Right hand, is called, the Place of Unites. Number in general, is by Euclid defined to be, liovd. S'av wocrorns, a Multitude, or Aggregate of Unites; and in this Sense Unity is not a Number But Unity as it may be taken for an Individual Unite - NL Unite, is certainly as much a Number as io,, oo, Qjc.

unity.c: UNITY of P off ejfion, in the Civil Law, is cal - led, Covfolidatio fruElus & proprietatis, and fig - nifies Joynt P off ejfion of two Rights by several Titles. As for Example: If I take a Lease of Land from one upon a certain Rent, and afterwards I buy the Fee - simple, this is an Unity of Pojfejjion, by which the Lease is extinguished, by reason that I, which before had the Occupation only for my Rent, am become Lord of the fame, and am to pay my Rent to none but my self.

universal.c: UNIVERSAL EquinoElial Dial, is made of two Rings of Brafsor Silver, that open and fold toge - ther, with a Bridge or Axis, and a Slider, and a little Ring to hang or hold it up by: it is divided on one side of the great Ring into Degrees, and sometimes on the other into two Quadrants, or Degrees, but one is enough: The Innermost Ring is divided into Hours, fub - divided on the Face and on the outside of the Ring, into every five Minutes. The Axis has the Suns De - clination on one side, and the Days of the Month and the Sun ’ s Place on the other. To Use it for the Hour, the Perpendicular Line ' or Stroke which is on the Slider, which moves on the outer Ring, must be fet to the Latitude of the Place, and the Hole in the Slider on the Bridge either to the Sun ’ s Place in the Ecliptick, the Day of the Month, or his Declination; and then the Rings being opened, and fet square to one ano - ther, move the Dyal about to and fro, till the Sun shine through the Hole, and on the Inner Edge of the Innermost Ring, and there it will shew the true Hour.

In this case, except the Demandant shall averr the contrary, he shall recover no Damages: When this Plea will serve to avoid Charges, and when not, fee Pfit ch - in sol..

urachus.c: URACHUS, is one of the Umbilical Vessels, being a small Membranous round Pipe, with a ve - ry strait Cavity arising from the bottom of the Bladder up to the Navel, out of which it passes along with the common Cover, and opens into the Allantoides of the Feet us: ’ Tis mere pervious in some of the larger Brutes than in Men, in whom some have denied it to be hollow; but that seems contradided by the Instances we have had of Mens making Water by the Navel, when the Passage of the Penis hath been quite stopped. Bartholin and some others fay, That the Vrachus in Men reaches no farther than the Navel: But how then comes that Humour into the Allantoides, which has per - fedly the fame Taste with the Urine in the Blad - der ? The mistake seems to arise from that wrong Notion, That a Humane Foetus hath no Allantois, which hath been by Needham and others sufficient - ly refuted. The Use of the Vrachus is to convey the Urine from the Bladder, of the Foetus, into the Allantoides, which is placed between the Chorion and the Am - nion,

ureter.c: URETER, is a Filiulous Membranaceous Ves - sel, which proceeds from both Reins, and opens between the Membranes of the Bladder, by which the Urine passes from the Reins to the Bladders Celfus calls it the White Vein.

urethraorfifiula.c: URETHRA, or Fifiula, is the Urinary PafTa - ges, whereby the Urine is discharged: It serves in Males also for the Ejedion of the Semen. The Seminal little Bladders, empty themselves into it by Holes at the beginning of it, when there is occasion which Bladders or Vessels are surrounded with Glandulous Prostates, perforated with several Holes to which there is a little piece of Flesh affix - ed. Blanchards. Mr. Cowper observes, That the Urethra hath a Corpus Cavernofum, like to that of the Penis, which you wilLfind described under the Words Corpora Cavernofa but this of the Urethra, differs much in Figure from them: The Superior part of this Corpus Cavernofum lying between the two Crura of the former, he calls But bus, from its Figure - it is covered with the Muf cuius Accelerator Vrince it possesseth all the lower part of the Urethra extend - ing its self in the Perineum it hath moreover, a Septum Intermedium ( tho ’ not taken notice of by, Anatomists, ) dividing the right side of the Bulbus from the left, which descending to the end of the Bulbous part, is there obliterated. The Use of this Septum is ( as Mr. Cowper thinks ) to dired the Refluent Blood to the exporting Duds, its two Veins that carry the Blood back. As this Corpus Cavernofum descends on the Infen - our part of the Urethra, it is lessened j but when it approaches the Extremities of the two other Cor pora Cavernofa it again dilates it self and covers them composing that Body which they call the Gians of Balanus.

urinoussalts.c: URINOUS Salts, are that Tribe of Volatile Salts drawn from Animal, or other Substances that are contrary to ilcids: And Mr. Boyle says, They are distinguishable from Lixiviate Salts, by this Test, That they will turn a Solution of Sublimate into a White Colour, whereas Lixiviate Salts turn it into a Y yellow one.

useinlaw.c: USE, in Law, properly signifies the Profits of Benefits of Lands or Tenements: for every Deed consists of principal Parts j namely, The Premises, and the Consequents. / U T R T he Fremifes, is the former part thereof, being all that which precedeth the Habendum, or Limi - tation of the Estate, which are the Persons contra - cting, and the thing contracted. The Consequent is that which follows the Premi - fes, and that is the Habendum., in which are two Limitations: The one of the Estate or Property, which the Party Paifive shall receive by the Deed: The other of the Vfe; which is to express in the said Habendum -, to or for what Vfe and Benefit he hall have the fame Estate, and of the Limitation of inch Vfes many Precedents are fet down in Law Books.

utlaryorvtlawry.c: UTLARY, or Vtlawry, is a Punishment for such as being called into Law, and lawfully fought, do contemptuously refuse to appear after an Origi - nal Writ, with a nihil habet, three Writs of Ca - pias,, Alias & Pluries, returned by the Sheriff non el inventus, and an Exigent with a Proclamation, thereupon awarded. And Bratton says, he muff be called at five Counties, a Month between every County; and if he appear not within that time, he shall be pronounced out of the Kings Protection, and deprived of the Benefit of the Law. The Ef - sect of this is divers; for if he be Outlawed at the Suit of another in a Civil Cause, he hall forfeit all his Goods and Chattels to the King. If upon Fe - long, then he shall forfeit all his Lands and Tene - ments which he hath in Fee, or for Life, and his Goods and Chattels. A Minor nor Woman can - not be Outlawed: For where a Man is said to be Outlawed, a Woman is termed Waived, UTRUM, See AJJife. U V u

utter.c: UTTER - BARRISTERS, are such, who sot their long Study, and great Industry be slow'd up - on the Knowledge of the Common Law, are cal - led from their Contemplation to Practice, and in the Face of the World, to take upon them the Pro - section and Defence of Clients; the time before any ought to be called to the Bar, was formerly eight Years, but now reduced tofeven and the Exercises done by him ( if he were not called. Ex gratis ) was Twelve Grand Moats performed in the Inns of Chancery, in the time of the Grand Readings, and Twenty four Petty Moats, at the InnS of Chancery, in the Term - times, before the Readers of the refpeCKve Inns of Chan - eery. A Barrifler newly called, is to attend the fix next long Vacations., the Exercises of the House, vi. in Lent and Summer, and is therefore for those three Years called, a Vacation Barrifler. And they are also called, Vtter - Barriflers, i e Pleaders without the Bar, to diftinguifii them from Benchers, or those that have been Readers, who are fometifnes admitted to plead within the Bar, as the Kings, Queens, or Prince ’ s Council are.

uveamembrana.c: UVEA Membrana five Tunica, is the forepart of the Choroides being almost altogether Continuous on the inside to the Tunica Sclerotis; it is persona - ted in the forepart, and leaves a space for the Ap - ple of the Eye, which may be contracted or dial - ted: Its exterior Surface is of various Colours, whence it is called Iris, and in this is the Diffe - rence of Mens Eyes as to Colour; as Black, Gray, &c. The Inside of this Uveous Tunick is cover ’ d with a Black Lining, that the Cavity of the Eye may be the parker.

uvula.c: UVULA, is a double Production of the Intern nal Membrane of the Mouth; its Substance is ve - ry lax, and it has a Number of small Glands as in the Palate: It is somewhat long and of a Conick Figure; it hangs from the Roof of the Mouth near the Passage Which comes from the Nose, above the Seat of the Larynx between the Tonsils: It is mo - ved by pair of Muscles, called Pterigoftaphiii - nus Externus & Internus: Its Use is to hinder Drink, &c. from falling down into the Aspera ar terra. use.c: USE - BOTE,. was formerly the Liberty a Tenant had to cut as much Wood on the Pre - misses as was necessary for the Support and Re - pair of the Farm House and adjoining Buildings. This is now call ’ d Ejlovers, Eftoverium.

USE in the Civil Law, is one of the Personal Services, and Signifies a Right that a Man hath of using a Corporeal thing belonging to another, without prejudice to the Proprietor of it; this Right is not so great as an VfhfruEi: For he that hath this Right, cannot take the Profits generally, but only for his daily Use and necessary Sub - fiftence.

undress.c: UNDRESS, did formerly signifie a Silver Penny; or a Sterling or Enfterling in a restrained Sense, and was so called, because coined only at London and not at the Country Mints.

Where theJDi - ringent a represents the Time, and the Lines a b ic, xd, ( c. the Uniform or Equable Velocities with which any Body is moved, in any Parts or Moments of Time. And the Parallelograms ac, cz, if, e, do truly represent the Spaces de - scribed or run thro ’, with the Velocity a b, in the Times a,, j,;,;, From the bare Consideration of which only ic will follow. a z S Te - rn - & f f E d Jp . That the Spaces described by any Moveable with an Equable or Uniform Velocity, are al - ways as the Times. For the Parallelograms a c, ad, ( c. having all the fame Altitude, muff be as their Bases bc cd ( c. . Or if the Times be equal, the Spaces must be as the Velocities that is the Parallelograms an to am, will be as ah to a /, ( c. . tV ' ' ' ’ ' . And from hence it will follow, that if the Spaces are as the Velocities, the Times will be e - qual; if as the Times, the Velocities will be equal. . Where the Spaces are equal, the Times must be reciprocally as Velocities; for the Similar and Parallel Rectangles have their sides reciprocally proportion - table and vice versa, where the Times and Veloci - ties are reciprocally proportionable, the Spaces must be equal. . Wherefore the Ratios of the Spaces are al - ways Compounded of the Patio s of the Times and Velocities: And consequently deducing the patio of the Time out of that of the Velocity or which is all one, dividing the Space by the Time, there will result the Velocity; dividing by the Velocity, the Quotient will be the Time. After much the fame manner also may the Uni - form or Equable Acceleration or Retardation of any Motion, be expressed very easily and dearly by Lines. As X E T B D YL L n N Ca H I K Ci As suppose m the right Lined A ABC, the side AB denotes the Time in which a Body may move from a point of Reft as in A: And having its Velocity continually encreasing in the Uni - form Ratio of the Lines DL, EL, FL and BC: or decreasing equally back again in the fame Ratio, from any determinate degree of it in BC, to none at all in A. In this Figure then the Triangles ALD, ALE, ASS, and ABC, will very appositely represent the Spaces described in the several Times AD, AE, AF, and AB;, and consequently the Trapezia DL, DC, &c. will represent the still aggregated Velocity, and the Spaces corresponding thereunto. And from hence all the Laws and Affe & ions of equable accelerated Motions, will be easily accounted for which are such asthefe, vi. . That the Space described at the end of the Accelerated Motion, will be equal to that which would have been described by an uniform equal Motion in the fame time, and with half the de - gree of Velocity which the accelerated Body did at last acquire: For j the A A C Br MB; Each being the half of the GB. . For the Area's of the similar A ALL, AEL, &c. are as the Squares of AD, AE, &c. . And comparing divers Motions, thus uni - formly accelerated one with another; it will be plain that the Spaces run thro ‘, will be to one ano - ther in a Compound Ratio of the Times, and of the greatest Velocities at any time acquired ( because similar A are in a Ratio compounded of that of their ( Ides. ) . And from hence ’ tis plain, that the Case of Bo - dies accelerating their Motion uniformly so as that the Spaces described, shall be as the Squares of the Times, ( which is the known case of the Descent, of heavy Bodies to wards the Centre of the Earth, ) may be very well exprest by the Complement of the Semi - parabola AEH. Where the Vertical Tangent AE, represents the determinate Time divided into equal Parts; and the Lines BO, CP, Dq, and EH, the several Ve - locities acquired in the several Descents. Now the Spaces described ABO, AC, &c. are as the Squares of the Times AB, AC, &c. that is, as the Squares f the Ordinates do, f p, g q, &c. which Squares are ( by the Parabola ) as the Abfcijr Ad, Af, Ag, &c. Wherefore the Velocities acquired at the end of any Descents, will be as the Squares of the Times in which these Descents are made. That is the Velocity at the end of the Second Moment or part of Time; to the Velocity at the end of the First Moment, will be as the Square of the Second to the Square of the First, or as the Fourth to the First, &c.

But Dr. Wallis in Philof. Trans. N.. tells us, that ' tis not the whole of the unstruck String that trembles, but the several Parts severally, according as they are Unifons to the whole, or the Parts of that String which is so ( truck. V. gr. If one String be an upper Odtave to another, and there - fore an Unison to each half of it when tis flops in the middle. Then I fay if the former be ( truck while the latter is open, the two halves only, f the latter will tremble, and not the middle Point, as you may easily try, by laying a bit of Paper lightly wrapt about the middle of the fe - cond String.
